body.statement:
For every finite \(\mathcal H_0\subset[-H,H]^K\), the fixed Gaussian grid experiment is exactly embedded by vertex controls in the score diffusion. For arbitrary predictable policies, including policies on zero-allocation faces, the discontinuous closed-test terminal loss satisfies
\[
\sup_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}|B_n(\lambda)-B(\lambda)|\longrightarrow0,
\qquad c_{n,m}\longrightarrow c_m\quad(1\leq m\leq M),
\qquad V_n\longrightarrow V.
\]
Moreover, for each \(\epsilon>0\) there are predictable finite-horizon policies whose scenario-risk vectors converge coordinatewise to that of an \(\epsilon\)-optimal diffusion control.
body.justification: It identifies the attainable local-power regret frontier for the fixed confirmatory test on every finite bounded scenario list and transfers a near-optimal diffusion risk vector to predictable finite-stage recruitment.
body.gap: The theorem is not positioned as an unqualified strict extension. Wager--Xu and Adusumilli supply regular-payoff diffusion architecture, while Araman--Caldentey supplies a low-information posterior-control donor; none supplies the boundary-stable discontinuous closed-test transfer proved here. The repository's multi-arm second-order minimax frontier is complementary because it concerns unrestricted finite-population binary-contrast design and estimation rather than fixed-test local-Gaussian subgroup recruitment.
body.consumer: It converts a continuum recruitment solution into asymptotically equivalent finite-stage policies for interAdapt-style subgroup-enrichment designs.
body.proof_tex:
Fix an arbitrary finite scenario list
\(\mathcal H_0=\{h^1,\ldots,h^M\}\subset[-H,H]^K\).  Only finiteness and
\(|h_j^m|\leq H\) are used below.

\emph{Exact embedding.}
Fix \(n\) and \(\pi_n\in\Pi_n\).  On
\(((i-1)/n,i/n]\), define the vertex control
\[
 u_j(t)=\mathbf 1\{A_i=j\}.
\tag{1}
\]
The randomization producing \(A_i\) is made at the left endpoint from
\(\mathcal F_{i-1}\).  Thus (1) is predictable by
\(\mathrm{ass{:}finite\mbox{-}predictability}\), and it belongs to
\(\mathcal U\) by
\(\mathrm{ass{:}continuous\mbox{-}observed\mbox{-}control}\) and
\(\mathrm{def{:}continuous\mbox{-}control\mbox{-}class}\).  Conditional on
the past and \(A_i=j\), the diffusion increments are
\[
 \Delta X_j=\frac{h_j^m}{n}
 +W_j(i/n)-W_j((i-1)/n)
 \sim\mathcal N\!\left(\frac{h_j^m}{n},\frac1n\right),
 \qquad \Delta Q_j=\frac1n,
\tag{2}
\]
and all other coordinates have zero increments.  By
\(\mathrm{ass{:}gaussian\mbox{-}known\mbox{-}variance}\) and
\(\mathrm{ass{:}local\mbox{-}scenario\mbox{-}scaling}\),
\(Y_i/\sqrt n\), conditionally on the same history and action, has exactly
the score law in (2).  Induction over \(i\) proves equality of the complete
observed score--clock laws under every scenario \(m\).  Consequently every
finite policy is embedded exactly as a vertex-control diffusion policy, with
the same scenario-risk vector.

\emph{Continuous-payoff approximation.}
Let \(g_m:\mathbb R^K\times[0,1]^K\to[0,1]\) be continuous for
\(m=1,\ldots,M\).  We first prove convergence of its prior-weighted value
over \(n\)-grid vertex controls to its value over \(\mathcal U\).
On the canonical observed space, a progressively measurable
\(\Delta(\mathcal J)\)-valued control \(u\) can be approximated by simple
predictable controls \(u^{(r)}\): approximate its bounded predictable
coordinates by simple predictable functions and project their vectors onto
the closed simplex.  Bounded convergence in measure gives
\[
 \mathbb E_0\int_0^1\sum_j
 |u_j^{(r)}(t)-u_j(t)|\,dt\longrightarrow0.
\tag{3}
\]
The inequality \((\sqrt a-\sqrt b)^2\leq |a-b|\), for \(a,b\geq0\),
and the Itô isometry show from (3) that the martingale parts of the score
vectors converge in \(L^2(\mathbb P_0)\); the clock vectors converge in
\(L^1(\mathbb P_0)\).  Since \(|h_j^m|\leq H\), the drift terms converge
in \(L^1\) under every scenario as well.

For a fixed simple control, subdivide each of its finitely many time cells
into \(n\)-grid cells.  At the left endpoint of a grid cell, choose vertex
\(j\) with the simplex probabilities prescribed by the simple control.
Within each time cell, the sum of the conditional variances of the
normalized centered allocation counts is at most the reciprocal of the
number of grid cells and hence tends to zero.  Conditional on those counts,
the coordinate score increment has mean \(h_j^m\Delta Q_j\), variance
\(\Delta Q_j\), and characteristic function
\[
 \exp\!\left\{\mathrm i z_jh_j^m\Delta Q_j
 -\frac12z_j^2\Delta Q_j\right\}.
\tag{4}
\]
At the finitely many decision times, each past-measurable action kernel can
be replaced by one continuous outside a set of arbitrarily small
\(\mathbb P_0\)-probability: approximate its bounded coordinate functions
by continuous functions off a small Borel set and project back onto the
simplex.  A union bound over the finitely many cells controls the probability
that any action changes.  Induction over the cells can then apply (4) at
continuity points.  Letting the exceptional probability vanish and then
using (3) yields a diagonal sequence of predictable grid policies
\(\pi_n[u]\) such that
\[
 (X_n,Q_n)\Longrightarrow(X^u(1),Q^u(1))
 \quad\text{under the zero-drift reference law}.
\tag{5}
\]
Vertex randomization allows a simplex coordinate to equal zero, so no
positive allocation lower bound has been added.

We transfer (5) to every declared scenario without treating the adaptive
clock as independent of the score.  Under the zero-drift reference law put
\[
 M_m(t)=\sum_jh_j^m\int_0^t\sqrt{u_j(s)}\,dW_j(s),
 \qquad
 A_m(t)=\langle M_m\rangle_t
 =\sum_j(h_j^m)^2Q_j(t).
\tag{6}
\]
Because \(\sum_jQ_j(1)=1\) and \(|h_j^m|\leq H\),
\[
 0\leq A_m(1)\leq H^2.
\tag{7}
\]
The likelihood ratio from the zero-drift law to scenario \(m\) is
\[
 Z_m(X(1),Q(1))
 =\exp\{M_m(1)-\tfrac12A_m(1)\}.
\tag{8}
\]
Its square factors pathwise as
\[
 Z_m(X(1),Q(1))^2
 =\underbrace{\exp\{2M_m(1)-2A_m(1)\}}_
 {\mathcal E(2M_m)_1}\exp\{A_m(1)\}.
\tag{9}
\]
This is a factorization, not an independence assertion.  Moreover,
\[
 \frac12\langle2M_m\rangle_1=2A_m(1)\leq2H^2.
\tag{10}
\]
For a simple predictable integrand, successive conditional Gaussian
expectations show that \(\mathbb E_0\mathcal E(2M_m)_1=1\).  For a general
progressively measurable control, approximate the bounded integrand in
\(L^2(dt\,d\mathbb P_0)\) by simple predictable integrands.  The stochastic
integrals and brackets then converge in probability.  If \(R\) is any such
simple approximating martingale with energy at most \(4H^2\), the same
factorization and the conditional Gaussian identity at doubled integrand
give
\[
 \mathbb E_0[\mathcal E(R)_1^2]
 =\mathbb E_0[\mathcal E(2R)_1e^{\langle R\rangle_1}]
 \leq e^{4H^2}.
\]
The exponentials are therefore uniformly integrable, and passage to the
limit preserves their mean one.  Combining this bounded-energy conclusion
with (7)--(9) gives the corrected adaptive-clock estimate
\[
 \mathbb E_0[Z_m(X(1),Q(1))^2]
 \leq e^{H^2}\mathbb E_0\mathcal E(2M_m)_1
 =e^{H^2}.
\tag{11}
\]
The same calculation holds for grid vertex controls, whose bracket is
\(\sum_j(h_j^m)^2Q_{j,n}\leq H^2\).  Hence the likelihood ratios of the
approximating controls are uniformly integrable.  Since
\[
 Z_m(x,q)=
 \exp\!\left\{\sum_jh_j^mx_j-\frac12
 \sum_j(h_j^m)^2q_j\right\}
\tag{12}
\]
is continuous, truncation of \(Z_m\), (5), and (11) imply
\[
 \begin{split}
 \mathbb E_m^{\pi_n[u]}g_m(X_n,Q_n)
 &=\mathbb E_0^{\pi_n[u]}[Z_m(X_n,Q_n)g_m(X_n,Q_n)]\\
 &\longrightarrow
 \mathbb E_0^u[Z_m(X(1),Q(1))g_m(X(1),Q(1))]\\
 &=\mathbb E_m^ug_m(X(1),Q(1)).
 \end{split}
\tag{13}
\]
Because \(M\) is finite, this convergence is simultaneous over all
scenarios.

Let \(G_n(\lambda)\) and \(G(\lambda)\) be the infimal prior-weighted risks
for the continuous payoffs \(g_m\), over \(\Pi_n\) and \(\mathcal U\),
respectively.  Exact embedding gives \(G(\lambda)\leq G_n(\lambda)\).
Conversely, choose a control within an arbitrary positive tolerance of
\(G(\lambda)\) and apply (13).  Therefore
\[
 G_n(\lambda)\longrightarrow G(\lambda).
\tag{14}
\]
For fixed \(\delta>0\), the envelope losses in
\(\mathrm{def{:}terminal\mbox{-}envelopes}\) are bounded and continuous:
exponentiation, finite arithmetic means, finite minima, and
\(f_\delta^\pm\) are continuous.  Thus (14) gives
\[
 B_{n,\delta}^{\pm}(\lambda)
 \longrightarrow B_\delta^{\pm}(\lambda).
\tag{15}
\]
For either sign and either experiment, the value is \(1\)-Lipschitz in
\(\lambda\) under the \(\ell_1\) norm because each scenario loss lies in
\([0,1]\).  A finite \(\ell_1\)-net of the compact simplex \(\Delta_M\),
followed by the two Lipschitz inequalities, upgrades (15) to
\[
 \sup_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}
 |B_{n,\delta}^{\pm}(\lambda)-B_\delta^{\pm}(\lambda)|
 \longrightarrow0.
\tag{16}
\]

\emph{Removal of the envelopes.}
The scalar inequalities
\(f_\delta^-\leq\mathbf1\{\,\cdot<0\,\}\leq f_\delta^+\) and
\(\mathrm{lem{:}quantitative\mbox{-}terminal\mbox{-}comparison}\) give
\[
 B_{n,\delta}^-(\lambda)\leq B_n(\lambda)\leq
 B_{n,\delta}^+(\lambda),\qquad
 B_\delta^-(\lambda)\leq B(\lambda)\leq
 B_\delta^+(\lambda),
\tag{17}
\]
and each upper-minus-lower width is at most
\(\rho_{H,K}(\delta,\eta)\), uniformly in \(n\) and \(\lambda\).
Combining (16)--(17), with \(\eta=\sqrt\delta\), yields
\[
 \limsup_{n\to\infty}\sup_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}
 |B_n(\lambda)-B(\lambda)|
 \leq \rho_{H,K}(\delta,\sqrt\delta).
\tag{18}
\]
The final assertion of
\(\mathrm{lem{:}quantitative\mbox{-}terminal\mbox{-}comparison}\) permits
\(\delta\downarrow0\), proving
\[
 \sup_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}|B_n(\lambda)-B(\lambda)|
 \longrightarrow0.
\tag{19}
\]
At the point-mass prior \(e_m\), the definitions give
\(B_n(e_m)=c_{n,m}\) and \(B(e_m)=c_m\).  Hence
\[
 \max_{1\leq m\leq M}|c_{n,m}-c_m|\longrightarrow0.
\tag{20}
\]

We next transfer the minimax regret.  Let \(C_n\) be the closure in
\([0,1]^M\) of the achievable finite-experiment regret vectors.
Exogenous randomization at time zero makes \(C_n\) convex, and it is compact.
If \(v_n=\min_{r\in C_n}\max_mr_m\), then
\(D_n=C_n+\mathbb R_+^M\) contains \(v_n\mathbf1\), whereas
\((v_n-a)\mathbf1\notin D_n\) for \(a>0\).  For
\(y_k=(v_n-k^{-1})\mathbf1\), let \(d_k\) minimize
\(\|y_k-d\|_2\) over \(d\in D_n\).  Convexity and minimality give
\[
 (d_k-y_k)^\top(d-d_k)\geq0\qquad(d\in D_n).
\]
Set \(\lambda_k=(d_k-y_k)/\|d_k-y_k\|_1\).  Since
\(D_n+\mathbb R_+^M=D_n\), substitution of \(d=d_k+ae_j\) shows that
\((\lambda_k)_j\geq0\), so \(\lambda_k\in\Delta_M\).
Furthermore, \(d_k\to v_n\mathbf1\), because
\(\|d_k-y_k\|_2\leq\sqrt M/k\).  Along a convergent subsequence
\(\lambda_k\to\lambda_n\in\Delta_M\), and passage to the limit gives
\(\lambda_n^\top(d-v_n\mathbf1)\geq0\) for every \(d\in D_n\).
Together with \(\lambda^\top r\leq\max_mr_m\), this proves
\[
 \inf_{r\in C_n}\max_mr_m
 =\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}\inf_{r\in C_n}\lambda^\top r.
\tag{21}
\]
Translation by the oracle vector yields
\[
 V_n=\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}
 \left\{B_n(\lambda)-\sum_m\lambda_mc_{n,m}\right\}.
\tag{22}
\]
The identical finite-dimensional argument for diffusion risks gives
\[
 V=\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}
 \left\{B(\lambda)-\sum_m\lambda_mc_m\right\}.
\tag{23}
\]
Equations (19)--(23) imply
\[
 |V_n-V|
 \leq\sup_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}|B_n(\lambda)-B(\lambda)|
 +\max_m|c_{n,m}-c_m|\longrightarrow0.
\tag{24}
\]

\emph{Predictable policy attainment.}
Fix \(\epsilon>0\).  By (20) and (24), choose \(N\) such that
\[
 |V_N-V|+\max_m|c_{N,m}-c_m|<\epsilon/3.
\tag{25}
\]
Choose \(\pi_N\in\Pi_N\) with
\[
 \max_m\{L_N(\pi_N,m)-c_{N,m}\}\leq V_N+\epsilon/3.
\tag{26}
\]
Embed \(\pi_N\) as the \(N\)-block vertex control \(u^\epsilon\) from
(1).  Equality of its scenario-risk vector and (25)--(26) give
\[
 \max_m r_m(u^\epsilon)\leq V+\epsilon.
\tag{27}
\]

It remains to approximate this control for the original discontinuous
loss.  Conditional on the exogenous randomization and on any action
sequence of positive conditional probability, the sampled Gaussian block
increments are absolutely continuous on their sampled coordinate
subspace.  A terminal threshold equality is a zero set of
\[
 \sum_{j\in I}\exp(X_j-Q_j/2)-20|I|.
\tag{28}
\]
If at least one coordinate \(j_0\in I\) was sampled, condition on all
sampled Gaussian coordinates except \(X_{j_0}\).  Equation (28) has at
most one solution for \(X_{j_0}\), while its conditional law has a density,
so equality has conditional probability zero.  If no coordinate in \(I\)
was sampled, the left side is \(|I|-20|I|\neq0\).  Fubini's identity and
the finiteness of \(\mathcal I\) therefore give
\[
 \Pr_m^{u^\epsilon}\{a_j(X(1),Q(1))=0
 \text{ for some }j\}=0
\quad(1\leq m\leq M).
\tag{29}
\]

For horizon \(n\), divide enrollment into \(N\) consecutive blocks whose
lengths differ from \(n/N\) by at most one, keep the subgroup selected by
\(\pi_N\) throughout each block, and supply its normalized Gaussian block
aggregate to the next decision kernel.  This rule is predictable by
\(\mathrm{ass{:}finite\mbox{-}predictability}\).  The block clock lengths
converge to \(1/N\), and the aggregates have their exact Gaussian laws;
induction over the fixed number \(N\) of blocks gives terminal-state
convergence to \(u^\epsilon\).  Decision kernels may first be modified on
sets of arbitrarily small probability, simultaneously under the finite
family of Gaussian history laws, so that the induction occurs at continuity
points.  By (29), neighborhoods of the finitely many threshold surfaces can
be chosen with arbitrarily small probability.  Off those neighborhoods the
terminal loss is continuous and bounded by one.  Weak convergence there,
followed by shrinking the neighborhoods, gives predictable policies
\(\pi_n^\epsilon\) satisfying
\[
 L_n(\pi_n^\epsilon,m)\longrightarrow L(u^\epsilon,m)
 \quad\text{for every }m.
\tag{30}
\]
Equations (27) and (30) prove the asserted coordinatewise risk-vector
transfer.  The construction permits zero block allocations.  Every step
used only the finite list and \(|h_j^m|\leq H\); null-boundary closure was
not used.
